articles.title: Cultura-Media Art and Techno-Media Art: Dual-Path Evolution in Japanese Media Art
articles.authors: Qi Jiang
articles.abstract: In the global context, Media Art faces persistent tensions between technological change and established systems of artistic classification, particularly when concepts travel across institutional and cultural contexts. In Japan, the tradition of bijutsu (fine art) historically confined media art to a relatively narrow experimental domain, while popular media such as anime, manga and games developed largely outside this framework. Drawing on document analysis, CiNii Research records and selected cases, this article examines how media art and Media Arts became differentiated and institutionally related in Japan. It proposes Cultura-Media Art and Techno-Media Art as two heuristic pathways for understanding the cultural institutionalisation of popular media and the development of technology-oriented artistic practice. The Cultura pathway highlights cultural legitimacy, public support and tensions between state branding and cultural production, while the Techno pathway examines technology as a constitutive condition of artistic operation and visibility. Finally, the article analyses the reorganisation of visibility after the suspension of the Japan Media Arts Festival’s annual open call in 2022, identifying a shift towards distributed support, exhibition and archival infrastructures.

articles.title: Longitudinal Associations Between Problematic Internet Use Components and Adolescents’ Quality of Life
articles.authors: Román Ronzón-Tirado, Joaquin Manuel González-Cabrera, Juan Manuel Machimbarrena, Esther Calvete
articles.abstract: Although problematic Internet use (PIU) has been increasingly associated with poorer health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in adolescents, longitudinal evidence examining the longitudinal associations between specific PIU components and HRQoL remains limited. Guided by the cognitive–behavioral model of PIU, this study investigated the longitudinal relationships between four PIU components (preference for online social interaction, mood regulation, deficient self-regulation, and negative consequences) and HRQoL across three time points. The sample comprised 2,616 Spanish adolescents. A random intercept cross-lagged panel model was employed to disentangle between-person from within-person associations between variables. At the between-person level, all PIU components were positively interrelated and negatively associated with HRQoL. At the within-person level, only deficits in self-regulation preceded subsequent increases in mood regulation. Additionally, deficits in self-regulation were the only PIU component to precede decreases in HRQoL over time. Bidirectional associations were also observed, as declines in HRQoL preceded worsening self-regulation deficits and negative consequences. These findings highlight the role of self-regulation deficits in PIU and their association with adolescent well-being, underscoring the importance of targeting self-regulation processes in prevention and intervention efforts.

articles.title: Does Fear of Missing Out Precede Problematic Internet Use, or the Reverse? A Two-Wave Cross-Lagged Study of Taiwanese Adolescents
articles.authors: Chi-Jung Sui, Mingchuan Hsieh, Ming-Hsueh Tsai
articles.abstract: Fear of missing out (FOMO), online social comparison, and problematic Internet use (PIU) are consistently correlated in adolescents, and influential models treat FOMO as a motivational antecedent of problematic use. This temporal ordering, however, has rarely been tested against its reverse. We analyzed the first two annual waves of the Taiwan i-Generation Panel Study ( N = 8,311; Grade 7 to Grade 8; 49 percent girls) and estimated a latent cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) of PIU symptoms, FOMO, and online social comparison, using the survey weights and jackknife replicate standard errors. PIU symptoms predicted later FOMO (standardized β = 0.12, p < 0.001), and FOMO predicted later PIU ( β = 0.06, p = 0.017). The difference between the two directions was not statistically significant (Δ β = 0.06, 95 percent confidence interval [−0.01, 0.12], p = 0.093), and this remained so across eight analytic specifications, in which the estimates varied depending on the measurement model. FOMO and social comparison also predicted each other in the primary model but not in the ordinal sensitivity analyses, whereas social comparison did not predict later PIU, and all cross-lagged associations were small. These prospective associations do not support treating FOMO only as an antecedent of problematic use, because problematic use also preceded FOMO. A two-wave design cannot separate within-person change from stable differences between adolescents, so the findings describe prospective associations and await replication across three or more waves.

articles.title: Bystanders’ attributions of gender-based cyberbullying: The role of bystander, victim, and transgressor gender
articles.authors: Emily Herry, Kelly Lynn Mulvey
articles.abstract: Bystanders can help stop cyberbullying, but before they can respond to victimization, they must assess why the victimization occurs. Drawing on Attribution Theory, the current study assessed young adults’ attributions concerning cyberbullying. It was expected that bystanders would be more likely to use internal than external attributions when assessing gender-based cyberbullying. Based on the Social Reasoning Developmental Model, it was also expected that gender group membership of the bystander, victim, and transgressor would play a role in the use of different attributions. 387 young adults (Mage = 19.05, SD = 1.35) from a U.S. university completed a survey where they were randomly assigned to scenarios depicting gender-based cyberbullying. Participants then provided written explanations as to why they believed the victimization occurred. A codebook was created and responses were coded using Thematic Analysis and analyzed using a 2 (Transgressor Gender) × 2 (Victim Gender) × 2 (Participant Gender) × 5 (Attribution: Discomfort, Jealousy, Insecurity, Gender Identity, External) mixed-model MANOVA. Findings indicate that participants largely attributed cyberbullying to certain internal causes (i.e., insecurity, gender) rather than external causes or other internal causes. The gender of the participant, the victim, and the transgressor also mattered. Participants attributed insecurity more frequently in same-gender cyberbullying and gender more often when a female transgressor targeted a male victim. Findings highlight the importance of group membership and internal attributions in shaping bystanders reasoning. The current study underscores the need for interventions addressing bystander misattributions in order to promoter more effective bystander responses

articles.title: Between calorie counting and “eating for the soul”: Mapping the contradictory dietary landscape of TikTok for 13-year-old girls
articles.authors: Michal Yaron, Nelly Elias
articles.abstract: Social media algorithms play a pivotal role in shaping children’s and adolescents’ dietary perceptions, yet existing research largely relies on active hashtag searches, which do not capture the algorithmically curated user experience. Adopting a naturalistic ethnographic approach, this study maps the dietary content delivered to simulated accounts of 13-year-old girls on TikTok’s “For You” page. Through a thematic interpretive analysis of 300 algorithmically recommended videos, the study identifies a fragmented dietary landscape defined by five conflicting discourses: (1) Information, promoting a simplistic, calorie- or protein-centric view of nutrition; (2) Inspiration, framing diet and weight loss as an aspirational lifestyle; (3) Feel-Good, glorifying emotional hedonism and indulgence; (4) Struggle, depicting the relationship with food as an ongoing battle; and (5) Disorder, highlighting the psychological distress of eating. The findings demonstrate that algorithmically curated feeds may expose young users to a contradictory discursive environment in which the body is simultaneously constructed as an object requiring continuous optimization and as a site of unrestrained emotional indulgence. Navigating this tension is complicated by idealized portrayals of success alongside the lived reality of dietary failure, thus creating fertile ground for the normalization of disordered eating patterns. By mapping these fragmented narratives, the study conceptualizes the digital foodscape on adolescent girls’ TikTok accounts as a media environment characterized by persistent dietary paradoxes.

articles.title: Rationalization or reactance: How psychological distance and efficacy beliefs moderate the effect of perceived inevitability on online privacy protection
articles.authors: Jian Rui, Jingzhong Xie
articles.abstract: By collecting user information, algorithms pose a severe threat to user privacy. However, increased incidents of privacy breaches do not necessarily motivate privacy protection behaviors. Drawing upon System Justification Theory and Construal Level Theory, this research aims to explain how individuals rationalize disengagement from online privacy protection. An online survey of Chinese users of e-commerce platforms (N = 534) reveals that temporal and social distances of online privacy invasion were negatively associated with perceived inevitability of this threat, which was negatively related to the intention to protect online privacy. Furthermore, the relationship between perceived inevitability and the protection intention was only significant at low levels of response efficacy. Self-efficacy did not moderate this relationship. Therefore, individuals disengage from online privacy protection because they perceive privacy threats approaching and as inevitable and do not think there is any effective method mitigating these threats. These findings demonstrate how low psychological distance of online privacy invasion and lack of response efficacy may deprive individuals from their agency in protecting privacy.

articles.title: Fostering constructive online news discussions: The role of anonymity and subjectivity in shaping perceived polarization in a Dutch sample of online commenters
articles.authors: Carla Anne Roos, Sara Bögels, Emiel Krahmer
articles.abstract: Online news discussions are often characterized by polarization and hostile interactions, which may discourage people from participating. This study examines whether two features of online comments influence how people perceive the polarization and disinhibition of commenters, as well as people’s own willingness to join discussions: sender anonymity and subjective phrasing, that is, explicitly phrasing an opinion as an opinion (e.g., “I think”, “In my opinion”). We conducted an experiment with a purposive subsample drawn from a representative general population sample of Dutch adults who self-reported to be currently or previously active in online news discussions (N = 294; repeated-measures, age range = 17–88 years). Participants evaluated manipulated comments to news articles about issues that were generally considered polarized in Dutch society. Sender anonymity did not affect perceived polarization, perceived disinhibition, or intentions to participate in discussions. Subjectivity, however, led participants to perceive comments as less polarized and less disinhibited. Although this did not increase participants’ intentions to join discussions, participants themselves used more subjective language when replying to subjectively phrased comments. These findings suggest that subtle changes in the way opinions are expressed can shape interaction norms in online discussions. Subjective phrasing may encourage more constructive communication styles to spread between users, even without top-down moderation or requirements for identity disclosure.

articles.title: Rumination, excessive reassurance seeking, depression, and problematic social media use
articles.authors: Jon Elhai, Tali Gazit, Christian Montag
articles.abstract: Depression and problematic social media use (PSMU) symptoms are robustly correlated. However, few studies have investigated cognitive or affective psychological mechanisms explaining why depressed individuals may develop PSMU. We analyzed cross-sectional web survey data collected from 388 American university students in 2025. We administered standardized measures of depression, rumination, excessive reassurance seeking (ERS; a maladaptive interpersonal strategy often used by depressed individuals to test social relationship strength), and problematic social media use. Using confirmatory factor analysis, we discovered good-fitting measurement models for these measures. Using structural equation modeling, we found that rumination’s brooding dimension was significantly related to both ERS and PSMU symptoms. ERS was also associated with PSMU severity. Analyses revealed that brooding indirectly accounted for relations between depression and PSMU severity. Furthermore, ERS accounted for relations between brooding and PSMU severity. Finally, we discovered that the path from brooding to ERS indirectly accounted for relations between depression and PSMU. Results provide support for cognitive/affective and coping mechanisms such as rumination and ERS that may explain relationships between depression and PSMU. We also place findings in context of a widely-studied theoretical model of problematic Internet use.

articles.title: Basic psychological need satisfaction and problematic gaming, mobile phone use, and social networking in adolescents: Disentangling between- and within-person associations
articles.authors: Xuan Xu, Haide Chen, Wan Zhao, Lingfeng Gao
articles.abstract: Basic psychological need satisfaction is often treated as a dynamic antecedent and consequence of adolescents’ problematic use of digital technologies. However, longitudinal associations may reflect stable differences between adolescents rather than changes occurring within the same adolescent. Using three-wave data from 1,024 Chinese adolescents assessed at six-month intervals, this study estimated multiple-indicator latent random-intercept cross-lagged panel models examining psychological need satisfaction in relation to Internet gaming disorder (IGD), problematic mobile phone use (PMPU), and social networking site addiction (SNSA) scores. At the between-person level, lower need satisfaction was associated with higher IGD, r = −.442, 95% CI [−.783, −.102], and PMPU, r = −.614, 95% CI [−.952, −.277]. The association with SNSA was negative but not statistically significant, r = −.431, 95% CI [−.926, .064]. None of the six-month cross-lagged paths was statistically significant. In dimension-specific models, FDR-adjusted between-person associations remained for competence and relatedness with IGD and PMPU, whereas none of the dimension-specific cross-lagged paths was statistically significant. Composite-score and classroom-cluster-robust analyses yielded the same general pattern. These findings refine the theoretical interpretation of the need and technology use association: At a six-month timescale, the clearest detected pattern was stable covariation between adolescents, whereas reciprocal cross-lagged within-person associations were not detected. Distinguishing these levels provides a more precise basis for separating enduring need-related vulnerability from shorter-term compensatory processes.

articles.title: Users vs. independent judges: Comparing perceived authorship and ownership in AI-supported collaborative writing
articles.authors: Joseph Fung, Kamryn Kadotani, Samantha McMichael, Virginia Kwan
articles.abstract: With the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in academic and creative settings, understanding how this technology impacts fundamental concepts of authorship and ownership is important to protect learning, maintain academic integrity, and establish clear policies. This study (N = 320; 18 to 44 years old, M = 19.55, SD = 2.39) utilized a 2 (user vs independent judge) x 4 (completely user generated; AI-generated and user edited 4 sentences; user chooses from 3 AI-generated options; completely AI generated) between-subjects design to examine how levels of Large Language Model (LLM) input affect attributions of authorship and ownership by both the users and the independent judges in a collaborative writing task. Findings reveal a significant inverse relationship between the level of LLM input and users’ reported ownership and authorship and a positive relationship between their attributions of ownership and authorship. Additionally, discrepancies emerged between users’ and judges’ attributions, particularly at high and low levels of LLM input, suggesting that third-party evaluators and users may use different factors in allocating credit. Furthermore, this research investigated the role of background factors such as users’ experience with AI, their attitudes toward AI, and their writing level in moderating the relationships between (1) AI input level and attributions of ownership and (2) attributions of ownership and authorship. The findings reveal the need to identify optimal levels of AI integration that support learning without diminishing students’ sense of authorship and to develop assessment strategies that address differences in attributions of ownership by users and independent judges. For policy, the observed differences in attribution demonstrate the complexities of assigning credit and responsibility in AI-assisted creative works.

articles.title: Socially reconnected or disconnected? Adolescents’ loneliness and problematic social media use following a smartphone ban in Dutch secondary schools
articles.authors: Sanyogita S. Khare, J. Loes Pouwels, Hanneke Hendriks, Roy Otten
articles.abstract: An increasing number of schools worldwide are implementing smartphone bans, yet there is limited empirical research on their implications for various aspects of youth socio-emotional functioning. The current study examined changes in secondary school students’ social and emotional loneliness and problematic social media use (PSMU) following a smartphone ban, and the extent to which these changes depended on students' initial levels of social avoidance and distress (SAD). Our sample included 982 students(Mage = 14.1 years, SD = 1.6) from two Dutch secondary schools implementing a full ban (smartphone use was prohibited during all school hours including breaks). Students completed questionnaires about loneliness, PSMU, and SAD before the ban (W1) and three months following the ban (W2). Data were analyzed using difference score and multiple regression analyses. Students used substantially less social media during school breaktimes post-ban compared to pre-ban. Further, we found a small mean-level increase in emotional loneliness from pre-ban to post-ban. While mean levels of social loneliness remained stable, higher baseline levels of SAD predicted increased social loneliness post-ban. There were no changes in PSMU at the mean level nor in relation to students’ baseline levels of SAD. Taken together, we did not find that a smartphone ban alleviates secondary school students’ loneliness and problematic social media use. On the contrary, such a ban may entail an initial adjustment period and may not be a one-size-fits-all solution for improving students’ socio-emotional functioning.

articles.title: The dynamic interplay between cyberchondria and health anxiety in online health information seeking: A four-wave longitudinal network analysis
articles.authors: Yuanli Liu, Zeyang Yang
articles.abstract: As online health information seeking becomes increasingly common, cyberchondria has emerged as a concern associated with people’s maladaptive health perceptions and quality of life. However, the longitudinal interplay between cyberchondria and related psychological factors remains unclear. This study used cross-lagged panel network analysis (CLPN) to examine the relationships between cyberchondria, health anxiety, problematic social media use (PSMU), security, health self-efficacy, and life satisfaction across four waves of longitudinal data from 722 participants. The initial three surveys were conducted at one-month intervals, with the final survey conducted six months later. Cyberchondria and health self-efficacy were the most influential nodes across multiple networks. Throughout all transition periods, bidirectional longitudinal predictive pathways exist between cyberchondria and health anxiety. Life satisfaction and security demonstrated notable influence in the network. Using a data-driven approach, the present study highlights a dynamic reinforcement pattern between cyberchondria and its correlates. Future research could further explore these pathways to provide new insights into the mechanisms of cyberchondria.

articles.title: Attachment to social media: Conceptualization, measurement, and examination of its proximity-seeking function
articles.authors: Or Zaplavi, Yair Amichai-Hamburger, Mario Mikulincer
articles.abstract: In two studies, social media was conceptualized as an attachment-like figure that users turn to for proximity in times of need. This approach addressed the theoretical gap regarding whether individuals form specific attachment orientations toward social media that shape relational patterns and online behaviors. Hypotheses predicted users seek social media proximity in distress and form domain-specific attachment orientations predicting engagement beyond global attachment. Study 1 predicted that a new scale, the Social Media Attachment Orientations (SMAO) scale, would show anxiety/avoidance factors, correlate moderately with the Experiences in Close Relationships (ECR) scale, and uniquely predict engagement and interpersonal goals (anxiety increasing, avoidance decreasing both). Study 2 predicted mortality salience would increase closeness/identification, with effects moderated by SMAO anxiety (exacerbating) and avoidance (inhibiting). In Study 1 (N = 495), the Social Media Attachment Orientations (SMAO) scale was developed and validated to assess attachment anxiety and avoidance toward social media. Factor analyses and regressions supported its two-factor structure, reliability, one-month stability, and incremental validity beyond global attachment orientations. In Study 2 (N = 117), exposure to a distressing condition (mortality salience) was manipulated to determine whether it increased users’ closeness and identification with social media and whether these effects were moderated by SMAO scores. Hierarchical regression examined the main and interactive effects of distress and SMAO orientations. Findings showed that the SMAO is a reliable, valid tool explaining engagement with social media beyond global attachment orientations. Users reported higher closeness to social media after distress (vs. control), moderated by SMAO avoidance. Results extend attachment theory to the digital realm, with implications for understanding online engagement and digital well-being.

articles.title: Is Europe tuning out? Selective news avoidance and low news consumption across 15 countries in the European Parliament elections
articles.authors: Svenja Schäfer, Sanne Tamboer, Sanne Kruikemeier, Rens Vliegenthart, Alice Hamilton, Annelien Van Remoortere, Susan Vermeer
articles.abstract: Keeping up with the news is essential for democracy, particularly around elections when citizens make voting decisions. However, in secondary elections like those for the European Parliament (EP), individuals often actively avoid election news or engage with it minimally. We surveyed 15 European countries before the 2024 EP elections ( N = 7633) to examine types of news avoidance, news consumption, and their individual- and country-level predictors. Findings reveal regional patterns: low news consumption is most prevalent in Northern Europe, while selective avoidance is more common in Southern and Eastern Europe. Country-level factors play a minimal role, with most variance explained at the individual level. Selective avoidance is linked to low interest and dissatisfaction with news coverage, while low news consumption is associated with lower interest and perceived EU competence. This suggests different types of news avoidance require tailored approaches to foster engagement with EP election news.

articles.title: Making Sense of Videogame Paradata
articles.authors: Olle Sköld
articles.abstract: This article introduces the notion of paradata to the setting of videogame research. Paradata is a term that signifies data that is informative about data processes and data practices. Drawing on existing paradata scholarship and two vignette studies of online videogame communities, the article explores how paradata can function as both a theoretical and practical resource, while also addressing its limitations. The findings conceptualize videogame paradata as a technologically underpinned and heterogeneous set of data and documentation that illuminates diverse practices and processes, including epistemic dimensions, environmental and social contexts, and procedures of data collection, processing, and use. The article argues that paradata offers a valuable framework for examining videogame processes and procedurality by enabling analysis of how multiple layers of videogame artifacts emerge alongside gameplay and related practices. Additionally, paradata helps conceptualize the fragmented nature of the epistemic world of videogames and play.

articles.title: Imagined Games by Real Historians
articles.authors: Renard Gluzman, Andrea Nanetti, Gerassimos D. Pagratis
articles.abstract: Historians are interested in games as a medium for communicating the past, but most lack a clear starting point for translating their research into game form. We designed and developed an online exercise to help historians take a first step towards a game concept without prior design expertise. We have tested a template at various academic levels, with full professors, associate professors, postdoctoral researchers and PhD candidates, using different research methods (e.g. interpretative, qualitative, quantitative). The results are imagined games, or game concepts, and we present three here. These examples show what historical games might look like and what this means for the historian's role in game creation. This paper points towards reclaiming the term historical games from its popular use in games media, a meaning that has also shaped much academic discussion.

articles.title: AI governance through the eyes of users: a large-scale study of online reviews
articles.authors: Stefan Pasch
articles.abstract: Purpose With the growing importance of artificial intelligence (AI) governance, numerous high-level frameworks have been articulated by policymakers and expert communities to guide the development and application of AI. While such frameworks offer valuable normative orientation, they may not fully capture the practical concerns of those who interact with AI systems in organizational and operational contexts. This study aims to address that gap by exploring bottom-up, user-centered perspectives on AI governance. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a bottom-up approach to explore how governance-relevant themes are expressed in user discourse. Drawing on over 100,000 user reviews of AI products from G2.com, we apply Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Topic Modeling (BERTopic) to extract latent themes and identify those most semantically related to AI governance. Findings The analysis reveals a wide range of governance-relevant topics spanning technical and non-technical domains. These include concerns across organizational processes, such as planning, coordination, and communication, as well as stages of the AI value chain, including deployment infrastructure, data handling, and analytics. The findings show overlap with institutional AI governance frameworks on issues like privacy and transparency, while surfacing overlooked areas such as project management, strategy development, and customer interaction. Originality/value This paper advances AI governance research by introducing a scalable method for identifying governance-relevant topics using semantic similarity and unsupervised topic modeling. It offers a novel, bottom-up mapping of governance concerns as expressed in user discourse, highlights both alignments and blind spots in existing frameworks, and demonstrates how bottom-up user perspectives complement existing AI governance frameworks by revealing governance dimensions that are salient in practice.

articles.title: Maintaining relations: digital communication in university hospitals in the context of the COVID-19 crisis
articles.authors: Charlotte Jewell, Christophe Dubois, François Pichault
articles.abstract: Purpose The COVID-19 crisis intensified digital communication within hospitals. Crisis communication is typically viewed as an instrumental organisational tool for efficient and strategic communication. Adopting a Communication as Constitutive of Organisation (CCO) perspective, this study examines how the entanglement between hospital actors and digital communication provides insights into the continuous constitution of University Hospitals during and beyond the COVID-19 crisis. It considers how evolving sociomaterial interactions reveal matters of concern within crisis communication practices. Design/methodology/approach This study employs a qualitative multiple case study approach, focusing on two University Hospitals in Belgium. A thematic analysis was conducted on focus group discussions from Hosp.A and, using interviews collected at Hosp.B, a second thematic analysis deepened the findings. Findings The findings underscore the significance of “presence” within the hospital's network, demonstrating how digital communication participated in sustaining connections during the crisis. This highlights that the hospital is constituted through interactions and that communicative interaction must be maintained in times of disruption. Digital communication also highlighted the concern for spaces of emotional togetherness within the crisis. After the crisis peak, digital communication was (re)negotiated. This reflects the dynamic relationship between hospital actors and digital communication and highlights the continuous navigation of their place through the matter(s) of concern(s) in the situated realities. Originality/value With a CCO lens, the ongoing (re)negotiation of the sociomaterial entanglement is explored to underpin matter(s) of concern that open avenues for digital crisis communication research and practice.

articles.title: Leveraging ChatGPT as a tool to self-manage psychological well-being: an affordance perspective
articles.authors: Polina Durneva, Yuan Zhang, Attila Hertelendy, J. Elliott Casal
articles.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore how users leverage tools based on large language models (LLMs) to self-manage psychological well-being. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on affordance theory, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 20 participants and analyzed their use of ChatGPT for psychological well-being using grounded theory techniques. Findings Users learned about ChatGPT's potential through external influences, experimentation, and prior experiences. As their understanding evolved, they actualized various affordances but also encountered barriers when repurposing the tool for psychological well-being. Originality/value This study provides an empirically grounded account of how individuals appropriate a general-purpose LLM for psychological well-being. It identifies context-specific patterns for further affordance research and proposes user-informed design guidelines for LLM-enabled chatbots.

articles.title: Association between internet non-use and mortality risk among older adults: the explanatory contribution of social integration
articles.authors: Patrícia Silva, Gina Voss, Alice Delerue Matos, Roberto Martinez-Pecino
articles.abstract: Purpose Digital exclusion has emerged as an important dimension of social exclusion among older adults and has been associated with adverse health outcomes. However, its association with all-cause mortality and the potential role of social integration remain unclear. This study examined whether recent internet non-use was associated with all-cause mortality and explored the potential contribution of social integration. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained from the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE), including 47,989 community-dwelling adults aged 50 years and older from 18 countries. Internet non-use was defined as no internet use during the previous seven days. Country-stratified Cox proportional hazards models examined the association between internet non-use and mortality, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics, depressive symptoms, and physical health. Mediation analyses evaluated the potential contribution of social integration. Findings Internet non-use was independently associated with a higher risk of all-cause mortality after adjustment for sociodemographic characteristics, depressive symptoms, and physical health. This association remained after accounting for social integration, although it was partially attenuated. Social integration explained part of the observed association, suggesting that it may represent a potential explanatory pathway linking internet non-use and mortality. Research limitations/implications Recent internet non-use was independently associated with higher all-cause mortality among older adults. Social integration accounted for part of this association, although additional pathways are likely to contribute. These findings support the interpretation of internet non-use as a marker of broader digital exclusion and highlight the importance of promoting digital inclusion and social participation in healthy ageing. Practical implications Policymakers should prioritize digital inclusion as a public health strategy. Programs promoting digital literacy and improving internet accessibility for older adults are essential not only for social integration but also as potential interventions to mitigate mortality risks associated with the digital divide. Social implications Non-use of the internet represents a critical barrier to contemporary social well-being. Addressing digital inequalities is a matter of social justice; fostering inclusive technological environments can enhance the social fabric and support the overall health and survival of aging populations. Originality/value This study extends previous research by examining, in a large multicountry European cohort, not only the association between recent internet non-use and all-cause mortality but also the potential explanatory contribution of social integration. These findings support the interpretation of internet non-use as a marker of broader digital exclusion and highlight the importance of promoting digital inclusion and social participation in healthy ageing.

articles.title: Beyond the Barrier of the Eco-Warrior
articles.authors: Roseline van Gogh
articles.abstract: Abstract: Media portrayals of eco-friendly people often display highly devoted eco-warriors. Although such portrayals may appeal to niche audiences, they make eco-friendly people appear distant and unrelatable to many others. Among young adults, highly devoted eco-warriors are admired for their dedication, yet frequently associated with negative traits, such as being pushy or judgmental. As these negative traits have become part of young adults’ existing cognitive schema of eco-friendly people (i.e., green people schema), they hesitate to identify with this group. Drawing on schema theory, this study investigates if media portrayals of eco-friendly people that challenge this narrow schema (i.e., schema-incongruent portrayals) improve young adults’ green people schema, and in turn, their eco-friendly group identity. In an online scenario-based experiment ( N = 174) using a one-factor mixed factorial design, participants saw Instagram portrayals of eco-friendly people that either confirmed or challenged the existing schema of highly devoted eco-warriors, representing the schema-congruent and schema-incongruent condition respectively. Results show that young adults’ green people schema only improved from pre-exposure to postexposure in the schema-incongruent condition. More specifically, young adults attributed fewer negative traits to eco-friendly people after seeing schema-incongruent (vs. schema-congruent) Instagram portrayals. This, in turn, related to stronger group identification. When young adults’ environmental self-identity was taken into account, the indirect effect of schema-incongruent portrayals on group identification through the green people schema was no longer significant, hinting that the effectiveness of schema-incongruent portrayals may depend on how eco-friendly individuals perceive themselves.

articles.title: Who Engages More, How, and Where? Examining Social Disparities in Multiplatform Social Media News Use Across Forty-Four Societies
articles.authors: Macau K. F. Mak, Michelle Le He, Leon Zhenglang Wang
articles.abstract: As more individuals adopt multiple social media platforms for news engagement, this study examines whether, how, and where sociodemographic disparities in multiplatform news use arise. Analyzing data from 2024, we find that women, older, less-educated, and low-income individuals use fewer platforms for news. Yet these disparities differ in nature: some groups adopt fewer platforms in general, others are less likely to use social media for news, and some experience both. Platform-level analyses largely mirror these patterns. Press freedom, polarization, and populism further shape these disparities. Robustness checks with data from earlier waves indicate that many patterns have persisted since 2018.

articles.title: Imagining the World Through News: A Cross-National Analysis of Country-Based Issue Ownership Networks
articles.authors: Zhuoyu Wang, Lei Guo, Mengmeng Wu, Chris J. Vargo
articles.abstract: This study examines how news media in different countries imagine the world and what accounts for cross-national similarity in these mediated worldviews. We introduce Country-based Issue Ownership Networks (CIONs), which conceptualize world imagination as associations between countries and issues in international news coverage. Drawing on 4,471,278 news articles from 42 countries, we construct two-mode country–issue networks and reveal their relational structure. We find a shared global foundation and three distinct communities of worldview. Economic interdependence is the dominant predictor of CION similarity, suggesting that cross-national world imagination is shaped primarily by a material logic.

articles.title: Fueling Distrust or Supporting the Navigation of Falsehoods? The Effects of Community Notes across Degrees of Deception on Credibility Perceptions and Content Engagement
articles.authors: Lina Buttgereit, Michael Hameleers, Katjana Gattermann, Andreas R.T. Schuck

articles.title: How Newsy is News? Development and Initial Validation of a Computational News Conventionality Index
articles.authors: Steen Steensen, Gunhild Ring Olsen, Lasha Kavtaradze, Bente Kalsnes

articles.title: Parents’ Perceived Sources of Adolescents’ Sexual Information and Sexting: Indirect Associations Through Parental Monitoring of Digital Media Activities
articles.authors: Robert S. Tokunaga, Paul J. Wright, Debby Herbenick

articles.authors: Wei Hong, Yixuan Niu, Weibing Yang, Xinyu Miao, Xiaomei Huang

articles.title: Mobile AI and the Making of Place: Black Spatial Production and Algorithmic Curation
articles.authors: Mikayla J. Renwick
articles.abstract: As mobile artificial intelligence (AI) systems become embedded in everyday technologies such as smartphones and social media platforms, it becomes critical to examine how they reshape the production of space, visibility, and belonging. This paper defines mobile AI as algorithmic systems that use real-time location and behavioral data to curate content, producing spatially situated experiences that encode racial and cultural assumptions about place. Rather than treating platforms as neutral intermediaries, I argue that mobile AI functions as a layered infrastructure—digital, sociotechnical, and spatial—that actively constructs racialized digital geographies while mediating access to representation and spatial meaning. Focusing on TikTok’s For You Page as a primary case, I demonstrate how platform algorithms leverage location metadata and engagement signals to generate “place profiles,” privileging content that is broadly legible and often aligned with outsider perspectives. In doing so, mobile AI amplifies narratives that flatten Black spatial knowledge while rendering culturally embedded, insider representations less visible. Extending Black geographic and critical race frameworks, I situate these dynamics within longer histories of spatial control, arguing that algorithmic systems reproduce racial inequality by determining whose presence is visible, whose movement is monitored, and whose culture is circulated in real time. At the same time, Black users engage these platforms as sites of active negotiation and resistance. Through strategic content creation, aesthetic choices, and narrative practices, they work within and against algorithmic constraints to assert spatial presence, archive community memory, and reimagine belonging. These practices constitute a form of digital placemaking in which cultural production becomes a means of reclaiming space across both physical and algorithmic terrains.

articles.title: Ports of illiberalism: Cross-platform diffusion of far right, conspiratorial, and reactionary Rumble videos on Facebook
articles.authors: Fatima Gaw, Chloe R. Mortenson, Hoda Fakhari, Rod Abhari, Inaya Fatima Hussain, Ayse D. Lokmanoglu, Erik C. Nisbet
articles.abstract: Alt-tech platforms like Rumble are a critical part of the illiberal public sphere where extremist and ideological communities converge. Despite their seeming isolation, alt-tech content penetrates big-tech platforms through parallel ports—socio-technical conduits that promote illiberal politics among mainstream audiences. This study develops an expanded typology of parallel ports based on their differentiated roles in cross-platform diffusion and applies it to the actor network sharing Rumble video links on Facebook. Using content and network analysis, it traces the systematic sharing of the most engaged Rumble video links from 2022 to 2023, identifying the actors and communities that sustain the Rumble–Facebook pipeline. Findings show that primary ports drive social media engagement while horizontal peripheral ports maintain ideological cohesion as central actors in the co-sharing network. Vertical peripheral ports, while less central, provide upward amplification. We discuss how alt-tech illiberal content penetrates big-tech platforms and its evolution as platform content moderation weakens.

articles.title: The fringification of funding: Monetization strategies within the Italian anti-mainstream Telegramsphere
articles.authors: Giovanni Boccia Artieri, Stefano Brilli, Valeria Donato, Nicola Righetti, Elisabetta Zurovac
articles.abstract: This study examines monetization practices within the Italian anti- mainstream Telegramsphere. By situating these practices within the rise of Alt-Tech platforms and “fringification” dynamics, the article contributes to understanding how fringe publics sustain themselves. Based on a sample of 454 channels collected via Telegram’s “similar channels” feature, we investigated monetization methods, and the discursive frames used to legitimize them. We identified nine categories of monetization tools, along with a spectrum of rewards ranging from material incentives to intangible benefits. Five primary discursive frames shape administrators’ appeals for financial support: support independent knowledge, join the fight, support for demanding work, sense of belonging, and hacks and insider deals. While mainstream digital economy tools such as PayPal, crowdfunding, and merchandise sales dominate, it is the discursive framing—more than the payment method—that constructs oppositional identity and legitimizes funding.

articles.title: ‘Are we going the way of screwtube?’: Alt-tech imaginaries, platform infrastructuralization, and Rumble use during the 2024 US presidential election
articles.authors: Anthony Kelly
articles.abstract: Alt-tech platforms constitute spaces of community building and ideological amplification for proponents of reactionary and far-right politics. As alt-tech platforms grow and scale, however, they can undergo infrastructural transformations—diversifying their operations while consolidating moderation, advertising, and governance practices. This can create tensions regarding user experiences and expectations of alt-tech. Drawing on a recursive, mixed-methods analysis of 76,280 user-generated replies to the videos of 3 leading pro-Trump influencers on the alt-tech platform Rumble in the period surrounding the 2024 US presidential election, this article describes how the ambits of alt-tech are discursively constituted in and through contestations over what can and should be done with media. Introducing the concept of alt-tech imaginaries to classify discursive articulations of the interests alt-tech platforms should serve, their proper relation(s) to authority, and the functionalities they should enable, the article addresses what happens when these ideas are confounded by infrastructural changes currently transforming Rumble.

articles.title: Movement to mass-murder: Understanding online radicalisation in the alt-tech ecosystem through the ‘Passages’ of users from 4chan to 8chan
articles.authors: Paul Jackson
articles.abstract: This article explores mass user migrations between two alt-tech platforms: 4chan and 8chan, as a result of instances of perceived deplatforming surrounding Gamergate in 2014 and a series of mass-shootings in 2019. It finds that deplatforming can intensify online radicalisation by pushing prohibited behaviours and users to platforms more suited to their purposes and compounding commitments to what is prohibited. The article introduces the concept of ‘passages’ to help illustrate how migration events affect migrating parties and destination environments, showing that users embed their motivation for migration into their use of a novel environment in processes of environmental selection, ideational entrenchment and behavioural extension. Analysis is based on a large-scale study of 4chan’s ‘Politically Incorrect’ board, using mixed digital methods, which sees platform design and users’ interpretation of technocratic features work together to co-create structures of meaning, with platforms affording users particular features and users according platforms particular powers.

articles.title: Deplatforming health misinformers: How telegram is leveraged to foster collective identity and shared purpose in the alt-health community
articles.authors: Nilou Davoudi, Jaigris Hodson, Victoria O’Meara
articles.abstract: As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, mainstream social media platforms like Facebook and Instagram attempted to curb the spread of health misinformation by deplatforming prominent groups that trade in conspiracy theories and “alt-health” misinformation. Telegram, known for its anti-censorship ethos, became an important alternative venue for this type of content and the groups that spread it. Through a case study analysis of one alt-health organization’s Telegram channel, this paper asks: What communicative tactics are used on Telegram to promote, legitimize, and grow alt-health organizations’ influence in the context of their deplatforming from mainstream social media? Four key findings are identified: (a) censorship is framed as a credential, rather than a social and political reprimand; (b) a politics of crisis is cultivated wherein democracy and freedom of speech are understood as subject to concerted and acute attack by powerful enemies; (c) elite collusion and corruption from governments and corporate actors are framed as pervasive; and (d) positive messaging cataloging wins and allied commentary from actors in traditional venues of power and authority are employed with increasing regularity over time. Taken together, we argue that deplatforming from mainstream social media and regrouping on alt-tech platforms such as Telegram offer specific sociotechnical and discursive opportunities that can be leveraged toward increasing legitimacy and epistemic authority for these organizations. Implications for the governance of social media with regard to health misinformation and conspiracy theories are discussed.

articles.title: Alt-tech everywhere: From fringe platforms to infrastructural condition
articles.authors: Marc Tuters, Eugenia Siapera
articles.abstract: This special issue argues that so-called “alt-tech” has shifted from a fringe platform ecosystem into a broader infrastructural condition shaping contemporary political communication. While earlier research treated alt-tech as a parallel system emerging in response to mainstream content moderation, the contributions collected here show how its core logics—permissive governance, affective intensification, symbolic compression, and cross-platform circulation—now operate across the wider media environment. Drawing on cases from the United States, Europe, Latin America, and China, the issue demonstrates how alternative and mainstream infrastructures have become increasingly entangled, with practices and repertoires moving laterally across platforms. This transformation challenges models of political communication centered on persuasion and informational correction, foregrounding instead participation, alignment, and the infrastructural shaping of visibility. Under these conditions, political meaning is increasingly shaped by environments that privilege antagonism, repetition, and affective intensification.

articles.title: Conspirative nudge: Visual dynamics, far-right engagement, and alt-tech infrastructures on Telegram during Brazil’s 2022 election day
articles.authors: Elias C. Bitencourt, Paulo F. C. Fonseca, Eurico Matos, Letícia Cesarino, Leonardo F. Nascimento
articles.abstract: This study investigates how images circulated in Brazilian far-right Telegram groups during the 2022 presidential runoff. Combining transformer-based computer-vision clustering with qualitative analysis, we analysed 5,384 unique images within 78,032 visual messages across 373 public groups and channels, derived from an initial data set of 126,640 messages collected during election day. We identified four interconnected dynamics – synchronization of informational flows, segmented emotional mobilization, epistemic legitimacy fabrication, and creation of cross-platform repositories – that anchor visual practices within Telegram’s alt-tech infrastructure. These dynamics configure a sociotechnical environment we conceptualize as a conspirative nudge: a latent, distributed state of affairs that facilitates emergence of conspiratorial practices by rendering certain interpretations more temporally aligned, affectively resonant, and visually actionable. Our framework extends debates in political communication and platform studies by foregrounding how platform affordances and visual artefacts jointly enact conspiratorial environments beyond deliberate intervention.

articles.title: Mirror worlds and misogyny: A mixed-methods analysis of incel discourse across mainstream and alt-tech platforms
articles.authors: Karmvir K Padda
articles.abstract: This article analyzes incel discourse as both an affective and ideological system across mainstream and alt-tech platforms, specifically Reddit and Incels.is. Drawing on a Computational Grounded Theory approach, I combine BERTopic modeling with qualitative thematic discourse analysis to examine how incel communities convert despair, humiliation, and rage into epistemic claims about gender, power, and justice. The analysis identifies three recurring formations: biologized rejection, the “foid” logic, and glorified violence, which persist across platforms despite stark differences in moderation and visibility. Building on Naomi Klein’s theory of the Mirror World, I argue that alt-tech spaces do not invent new ideologies but stabilize, intensify, and ritualize misogynistic extremism. Incel discourse is not merely descriptive; it is productive, ontologizing emotional pain and transforming grievance into knowledge through repetition, resonance, and digital infrastructures. Conceptualized as an affective epistemology, this system shows how misogyny is foundational, making violence feel not only imaginable but morally justified.

articles.title: Reappropriating the old platform: Nested alternative practices in Chinese alt-tech spaces
articles.authors: Luming Zhao, Xinyan Wang
articles.abstract: Recent scholarship on alt-tech emphasizes two formation paths: secession outside the mainstream and contestation within it. Building on this, we articulate an untheorized pathway: subsistence within the legacy platform. Drawing upon Shove’s social practice theory and employing netnography with 32 interviews, we examine China’s Tieba. Findings indicate that nostalgia for past Internet practices anchors further practice. Core members utilize Tieba’s BBS architecture and governance to appropriate part of this nominally neutral platform into alternative discursive spaces. We conceptualize this path as nested alternativity: (1) structural nesting, or embedding communities deep within platform hierarchies to maintain low visibility; and (2) discursive nesting, or subsisting through political compliance while pushing sociocultural boundaries. This case study foregrounds alt-tech not merely as a site property, but as a practice property, especially where political and economic constraints limit options.

articles.title: Politics after persuasion: Reactionary politics in feed-based media environments – a conversation
articles.authors: Alan Finlayson, Robert Topinka, Marc Tuters, Eugenia Siapera
articles.abstract: This article examines the transformation of political communication in feed-based media environments through a conversation with Alan Finlayson and Rob Topinka. It argues that prevailing models of persuasion are insufficient for understanding contemporary digital politics, where participation, repetition, and alignment increasingly structure how meaning is encountered. Rather than focusing on the transmission of messages, the discussion highlights how platform infrastructures organize communicative environments that shape orientation, affect, and political identification. Within these conditions, reactionary political forms appear particularly well suited to the logics of visibility, antagonism, and engagement that characterize contemporary platforms. The conversation situates these developments in relation to media and cultural theory, emphasizing the role of communicative environments in shaping plausibility and belief. The article concludes by considering implications for platform governance, suggesting that regulatory approaches oriented toward discrete actors struggle to address forms of influence that operate through distributed and infrastructural dynamics.

articles.title: Do People Believe a Significant Other Means Significant Savings? Lay Beliefs About the Financial Cost of Relationships
articles.authors: Johanna Peetz, Geoff MacDonald
articles.abstract: People in relationships tend to be in a better financial position than people who are single due to income pooling, joint purchase savings, and cheaper leisure habits. Across three studies (combined N = 1058 US Americans), we examine single people's beliefs about whether romantic relationships save money or cost money relative to singlehood. Across studies, participants (especially men) tended to endorse beliefs that relationships cost money. Lay beliefs regarding the financial cost of relationships were negatively linked to relationship readiness and intent to find a partner in the next 6 months (Studies 1–3), suggesting these financial beliefs dissuade singles from partnering. Notably, implicit theories about the cost of relationships could be shifted: When participants were induced to focus on financial advantages (Studies 2 and 3), participants' beliefs in the costliness of relationships were attenuated, and there was a small condition effect on higher relationship readiness and intent to partner across studies. In sum, implicit theories about the financial cost of relationships appear to play a role in decisions about staying single versus partnering.

articles.title: Observational Analysis of Communication Patterns and Stress Dynamics: Insights From a Relationship Education Program Designed for Partnered Sexually Diverse Individuals
articles.authors: Esther Liekmeier, Casey J. Totenhagen, Guy Bodenmann, Ashley K. Randall
articles.abstract: Stress communication and provision of partner support are important for relationship functioning. The Couples Coping Enhancement Training‐Sexual Minority Stress (CCET‐SMS) is a five‐module program designed to teach partnered sexually diverse individuals how to communicate and cope with stress and particularly teaching couples the 3‐phase method. The 3‐phase method is a structured and facilitated communication exercise aimed at strengthening couples' dyadic coping skills and has been found effective in decreasing perceptions of stress and ultimately increasing relationship satisfaction. However, the fidelity (and efficacy) of this method has relied solely on partners' self‐report measures. Because of this, little is known about how partners' turn‐taking behaviors and communication patterns unfold in real‐time when applying the 3‐phase method, and whether such patterns may reflect dynamics of stress regulation and coping processes. Using video‐recorded conversation data from eight couples practicing the 3‐phase method, this study applied conversation analysis with a dynamic dyadic systems perspective. Data were coded to analyze partners' turn‐taking behaviors. Results indicated that partners engaged in patterns of interaction characterized by stress exploration and supportive communication, including behaviors such as clarification, acknowledgement, and expressions of understanding. Limitations and future directions are presented.

articles.title: Curating Trust: Education, Museum Visits, and Trust in Scientists
articles.authors: Alexandra Valerie Dicks, Ricarda Ullrich, Martin Merkt, Gun-Brit Thoma, Kathrin Grotz, Patricia Rahemipour, Olaf Köller
articles.abstract: Trust in scientists is an indispensable condition in a modern knowledge society. Yet, the role of informal learning in museums in shaping trust is not well understood. We investigated how formal education and museum visit frequency relate to trust in scientists using two large data sets: one sample was drawn from a German-speaking population ( N = 1,066), and the other from visitors to 22 German and Austrian museums ( N = 14,026). Regression analyses showed a positive association between formal education and trust in scientists. Notably, we found a significant interaction between formal and informal education, indicating that the positive association between formal education and trust was weaker among more frequent museum visitors. Effects varied across museum types, underscoring the importance of institutional context. Our study highlights the potential of cultural and informal learning to help reduce educational inequalities in trust in scientists and promote more inclusive trust relationships.

articles.title: Beyond Correcting Misinformation: Science Communication and the Ethical Imperative to Strengthen Information Resilience
articles.authors: Christopher Cummings
articles.abstract: Science communication operates within information environments shaped by uncertainty, fragmentation, competing values, and information disorder. This conceptual commentary develops information resilience as a system-level capacity to support informed judgment, resist consequential distortion, preserve legitimate uncertainty and disagreement, and adapt as knowledge changes. It advances an ethical imperative for institutions with epistemic and communicative power to strengthen the informational conditions they help shape. Five institutional practices are proposed to strengthen information resilience by making science communication environments more anticipatory, assessable, contestable, responsive, and adaptive.

articles.title: Prevalence or Threat? How Misinformation Interventions Shape Veracity Discernment and Trust in Scientists
articles.authors: Myojung Chung, S. Mo Jones-Jang, Betty S. Lai
articles.abstract: Science misinformation poses two distinct problems: promoting inaccurate scientific beliefs and undermining trust in scientists. Yet little research has examined the psychological mechanisms through which interventions may address both problems. An experiment ( N = 832) compared accuracy prompts and threat-focused and efficacy-focused forewarning, examining perceived misinformation prevalence and threat as mediators. Both forewarning messages increased perceived prevalence and threat, but only threat was associated with better veracity discernment and greater trust in scientists. The findings highlight the importance of distinguishing how widespread misinformation seems from how harmful it feels when examining how interventions shape veracity discernment and trust in scientists.

articles.title: Work-Related Predictors and Outcomes of Different Forms of Scientists’ Science Communication Motivation—Exploring the Value of Self-Determination Theory in Science Communication Research
articles.authors: Lennart Banse, Julian Fick, Friederike Hendriks
articles.abstract: Using self-determination theory, this study conceptualizes science communication as an emerging professional role for scientists. We examine how organizational support and normative pressure relate to scientists’ motivational regulation and how autonomous and controlled motivation are associated with role prioritization and communication effort. Based on a cross-disciplinary survey of German scientists ( N = 1,331), autonomous motivation was strongly associated with both outcomes, whereas controlled motivation showed no positive associations. Links between workplace factors and motivation were less consistent: organizational support only weakly predicted autonomous motivation, whereas normative and formal pressure were associated with both motivation types. Findings highlight differentiated regulation pathways.

articles.title: Managing Visibility in the Gray Zone: Quasi-Visibility and the Relational Practice of Algorithmic Resistance
articles.authors: Boyuan Huangfu
articles.abstract: This article introduces the concept of quasi-visibility—a suspended, in-between condition that is neither fully visible nor entirely invisible—to challenge the binary presumption that has long dominated algorithmic visibility research. Drawing on textual analysis of 2,093 original Weibo posts and participant observation of the “naked child” incident, this study examines how algorithmic resistance unfolds under conditions of quasi-visibility. Our findings reveal two interconnected dimensions. In the actional dimension, users continuously recalibrate resistance through spatial appropriation and discursive maneuvering. In the relational dimension, they negotiate tensions with multiple actors through identity construction, boundary demarcation, and platform contestation. Theoretically, the article advances algorithmic resistance from a binary struggle “against invisibility” to a sustained practice of “managing visibility in the gray zone.” By foregrounding the lived experience of quasi-visibility, this study reveals how algorithmic resistance in China is not a unified collective act but a creative, sometimes concealed, and ambiguous political practice co-shaped by user groups, state censorship, platform governance, and the traffic economy.

articles.title: Virtual Reality Live-Streaming in China: Mandated Social Presence and Civilised Body
articles.authors: Xinyang Zhao, Pengfei Fu, Zhuyun Song, Xuefang Xie, Yitong Huang
articles.abstract: While emerging digital technologies such as virtual reality (VR) have generated significant economic benefits, they raise concerns about the potential harm to social norms and morals in digital spaces. Following ByteDance’s acquisition of PICO and the launch of its VR live-streaming platform, this article investigates how VR impacts user experiences and social interactions, running counter to China’s civilised internet policy. It employs autoethnography and semi-structured interviews with users to analyse the phenomenon of cabian , sexually suggestive content in China’s VR live-streaming. The social presence of VR complicates the existing form of social interactions, enabling voyeuristic experiences that blur privacy and intimacy. VR live-streaming, thus, manifests as vulgarity, reinforcing stigmas against nonurban and underclass populations. This article sheds light on the implications of emerging technology, which may appear neutral, for the ethical challenges and stigmatisation in social interactions when intertwined with certain cultural frameworks and policies.

articles.title: Digital Migration and Cross-Cultural Adaptation: #CatTax Culture as a Bridge for TikTok Refugees on Rednote
articles.authors: Chenyu Ni
articles.abstract: In 2025, due to considerations of data privacy and national security, the U.S. government banned the use of TikTok, causing many American users to switch to the Chinese social media platform Rednote and label themselves as TikTok refugees. This study focuses on the cross-cultural adaptation strategies of these migrant users, especially how the #cattax phenomenon became an important medium for them to adapt to Rednote’s culture. Based on high-/low-context cultural theory and social semiotics, this study employs multimodal analysis and thematic analysis methods to interpret user-generated posts. It found that migrant TikTok users conveyed kindness by sharing cat photos to win acceptance from Rednote’s local users. They adjusted their language and expressions to incorporate a mix of English and Chinese languages and local cultural symbols to fit into the community. In addition, cats, as emotional symbols, transformed migrant users into new members of the Rednote community. Most notably, not only did these users effectively fit into the Rednote culture, but they also transformed its social etiquette. They expanded the #cattax to a broader “pet tax” tradition, through which they changed the way they interact with local users. This study shows that although the TikTok ban originated from policy conflicts between governments, ordinary users established emotional bonds across political divides on social media, demonstrating spontaneous cultural integration.

articles.title: Correctness Costs Credibility? The Emotional Loop in AI-Powered Fact-Checking
articles.authors: Wenbo Zhao, Jingtai Tang
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for fact-checking, but the role of emotion in this process remains unclear. We propose an Emotional Loop in LLM-based fact-checking, in which the emotional cues in user prompts influence model responses, while the emotional tone of those responses shapes users’ subsequent evaluations. Across three studies, we examine this process in the context of partially false claims. Study 1 audits four widely accessible LLMs across 24,000 responses and shows that emotional prompts—especially negative ones—can improve LLMs’ accuracy in identifying partially false claims while also increasing the emotional intensity of their outputs. Studies 2 and 3 ( N = 400 and 299, respectively) examine how users evaluate emotionally framed LLM fact-checks. Across both studies, these evaluations depended on users’ own emotions. In particular, negatively toned replies undermined perceived credibility among users experiencing negative emotion. Together, these findings reveal what we term a “correctness costs credibility” paradox in the Emotional Loop: Emotional input can sharpen fact-checking judgments, while emotional spillover into model output may reduce perceived credibility under certain conditions. The Emotional Loop offers a process account of how emotion operates throughout artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated verification, highlighting the importance of considering both model performance and user reception in LLM-based fact-checking.

articles.title: Navigating Ecological Distress: A Multimodal Ethnography of #EcoAnxiety and #ClimateAnxiety on Instagram
articles.authors: Christian A. Palacios Haugestad
articles.abstract: Social media platforms are increasingly important in shaping environmental discourse. Yet, as ecological distress is folded into the logics of social media, there is a risk that therapeutic framings might depoliticize the crisis, reducing systemic threats to individual affect management. Analyzing posts associated with #EcoAnxiety and #ClimateAnxiety, this study investigates how ecological distress is constructed, performed, and contested on Instagram. Through a patchwork digital (auto)ethnography complemented by a multimodal critical discourse analysis, my research identifies three visual interpretative repertoires employed by creators: (a) the eco-influencers’ emotional confessional , which normalizes eco-anxiety through environmental aesthetics and affective disclosure; (b) the environmentalist psychoeducational slideshow , which legitimizes eco-anxiety as an ontologically real condition while calling for political action; and (c) the irreverent environmentalist post , which critiques therapeutic framings and toxic positivity through satirical humor. These repertoires offer distinct subject positions to viewers, ranging from the self-managed mindful eco-worrier to the empowered eco-worrier and the satirical critic . Moving beyond a strict binary that pits depoliticizing, individualized coping against collective political engagement, the study illustrates a complex “both/and” dynamic. The results demonstrate that when the anticipation of planetary degradation is mediated as affective pedagogy into the platform’s attention economy, its therapeutic management can operate not only as a neoliberal distraction, but as a form of radical self-care and political endurance necessary to sustain civic engagement. Ultimately, the study contributes to understanding the digitally mediated normativity of ecological distress, illustrating how the construction of eco-anxiety on Instagram can validate individual distress while laying groundwork for affective solidarity.

articles.title: AI-enhanced efficiency and AI-enabled cognitive offloading in Chatbot use: Associations with school performance among adolescents and emerging adults
articles.authors: Christine Liebenwein, Alexandra Wölfle, Desirée Schmuck

articles.title: Digital cultural capital and the creator economy: Bourdieusian resources, structural inequality, and platform-mediated cultural production
articles.authors: Jing-Yun Zeng, ZhengJun Jin, Xuxu Jin, Hong Li, Chang-Hyun Jin

articles.title: The Promises and Limits of Solutions Journalism: How Controversy Conditions Effects on Emotions and Attitudes in Response to News About Climate Change
articles.authors: Adam Shehata, Kim Andersen, Mats Ekström, Emil Östlund
articles.abstract: This study addresses an argument not considered in previous research on solutions journalism: that the emotional and attitudinal effects of solutions-focused news stories depend on the level of controversy of the solutions presented. Across two identically designed experiments focusing on reducing emissions from meat production (Study 1) and transportation (Study 2), we find that the promises of solutions journalism are conditioned by the real-world sociopolitical context in which it is embedded. Both levels of controversy and political predispositions among news consumers condition the effects of solutions journalism on the audience, even generating evidence of backfiring effects.

articles.title: Book review: Multimodality and Time: A Social Semiotic Approach VAN LEEUWENTHEO, Multimodality and Time: A Social Semiotic Approach. London and New York: Routledge, 2025. 152 pp. ISBN 9781032560328 (Hardback), ISBN 9781032541631 (Paperback), ISBN 9781003433453 (E-book). DOI: 10.4324/9781003433453
articles.authors: HENRIKA FLORÉN
